SOURCE: "Latent Collaboration in Multi-Agent Systems" (LatentMAS), Jiaru Zou, Ruizhong Qiu, Gaotang Li, Xiyuan Yang, Katherine Tieu, Pan Lu, Ke Shen, Hanghang Tong, Yejin Choi, Jingrui He, James Zou, Mengdi Wang, Ling Yang. Proceedings of the 43rd ICML, Seoul, PMLR 306, 2026. The PDF is arXiv:2511.20639v4 [cs.CL], dated 3 Aug 2026. Project code is at github.com/Gen-Verse/LatentMAS.

COVERAGE: 35 pages, 113,577 chars. I read the main text (about chars 0–30k), all of Sections 1–7, and the appendix text from A through G plus H (offsets about 55k–87k). The case studies I (about 87k), J (about 94k) and K (prompt templates, about 102k) I did not read in detail, and I only skimmed the references. The proofs in A and B were not checked line by line. The extraction was clean and not garbled. The appendix C.2 tail was not read (it covers the evaluation protocol). Page numbers below are PDF pages as printed.

CLAIMS
1. LatentMAS lets LLM agents collaborate without any text between them, and needs no training.
   - Each agent runs m auto-regressive steps on last-layer hidden states ("latent thoughts"). The layer-wise KV cache is then handed to the next agent, and only the last agent decodes text.
   - number: none
   - setup: sequential (planner, critic, refiner, solver) and hierarchical (code, math and science agents feeding a summarizer) MAS. KV caches are concatenated through HuggingFace `past_key_values`. Every agent must share the same transformer shape.
   - quote: "we extract the KV-caches from all L transformer layers of A1 once and collect the latent working memory of A1" and "with only the last agent decoding the final answer in texts"
   - where: p4–5, Sec 3.2–3.3

2. Headline result: accuracy, token and speed gains over a single model and over text-based MAS.
   - number: up to +14.6% accuracy; 70.8%–83.7% fewer output tokens; 4×–4.3× faster
   - setup: 9 benchmarks, 5 backbones (Qwen3 4B/8B/14B, Llama3 3B/8B), sequential and hierarchical settings. Mean of 3 runs, temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, 8×A100-80G.
   - quote: "LatentMAS consistently improves over the single-model baseline by an average of 14.6% and 13.3% under the sequential and hierarchical settings, respectively, and further yields gains of 2.8% and 4.6% over text-based MAS."
   - where: p6, Sec 4.1

3. The accuracy gain over text MAS is small, and often negative or zero on the easy tasks. Most of the benefit is cost.
   - number: Qwen3-8B sequential ARC-E 99.1 (TextMAS) vs 98.8 (LatentMAS); HumanEval+ 80.5 vs 80.5; Qwen3-4B GSM8K 89.8 vs 88.2. Across all tables, LatentMAS beats TextMAS by 5.4 points at most (Qwen3-14B HumanEval+: 81.1 to 86.5).
   - quote: "Acc. 82.4 89.8 88.2↓1.6 81.1 92.393.8 ↑1.5 83.7 93.895.2 ↑1.4" (GSM8K row)
   - where: p6 Table 1. Table 3, p22, also shows several ties and small drops.

4. Speed holds against an optimised baseline.
   - number: 2.6×–7× over vLLM-optimised TextMAS. Fewer than 50 latent steps match or beat TextMAS on AIME24/25, where TextMAS needs more than 20K output tokens.
   - setup: all baselines and LatentMAS also run on vLLM with prefix caching and tensor parallelism.
   - quote: "even after accelerating the TextMAS baselines using the vLLM service, LatentMAS still achieves a 2.6×-7× speedup over the vLLM-optimized TextMAS."
   - where: p7, Sec 4.2

5. Token savings.
   - number: 59.4%–87.9% fewer than TextMAS; 15.0%–60.3% fewer than a single agent. On the final agent alone, the average reduction is 29.1%.
   - setup: total output tokens; Table 5 (p24) covers the final agent only, for ARC-C, GSM8K, MedQA, HumanEval+ and GPQA-D, at 4B/8B/14B.
   - quote: "LatentMAS reduces token usage by 59.4%-87.9% compared with TextMAS" and "with an average reduction of 29.1%"
   - where: p7 and p24

6. Reasoning-heavy tasks (Table 2, p7).
   - number: Qwen3-14B hierarchical AIME24 63.3 (single), 70.0 (TextMAS), 73.3 (LatentMAS). AIME25 56.7, 66.7, 66.7. GPQA-Diamond 48.5, 52.0, 53.0. Qwen3-8B sequential AIME24 50.0, 53.3, 56.7.
   - setup: only Qwen3-8B and 14B. Max output 20,000 tokens for AIME and 8,192 for GPQA. AIME has only 30 questions per year.
   - quote: "Acc. 50.0 53.3 53.3↑0.0 63.3 70.073.3 ↑3.3" (hierarchical AIME24)
   - where: p7

7. Both halves of the method are needed, shown by a hybrid ablation (Qwen3-8B).
   - number: GSM8K / MBPP+ / MedQA: latent reasoning with text communication 85.5 / 66.4 / 65.9; text reasoning with latent communication 90.1 / 68.0 / 71.2; full LatentMAS 93.8 / 74.6 / 75.3.
   - quote: "Latent Reasoning + Text Communication 85.5 66.4 65.9 ... LatentMAS 93.8 74.6 75.3" (the first-variant text communication passes "only the last 128 decoded tokens")
   - where: p25–26, Table 7

8. The alignment matrix Wa helps.
   - number: +2.3% to +5.3% accuracy on 3 tasks (Figure 7), with the per-task bars read as +3.6%, +2.3% and +5.3%.
   - setup: Wa ≈ W_out† W_in, computed once per run and reused; d_h × d_h (the paper gives d_h=1024 for Qwen3-0.6B). Without it, last-layer hidden states drift out of the input-embedding distribution.
   - quote: "observe consistent accuracy gains of 2.3%-5.3% by Wa"
   - where: p3 and p8

9. Latent-step depth: accuracy peaks around 40–80 steps on Qwen3-14B, then plateaus or declines. The paper says too many steps adds "redundant or less useful information".
   - number: 40–80 steps
   - setup: three tasks, Qwen3-14B (Figure 8). The grid is m ∈ {0,10,20,40,80}.
   - where: p9

10. Theory.
    - Thm 3.1: text needs Ω(d_h·m / log|V|) tokens to express m latent steps losslessly. This assumes the Linear Representation Hypothesis.
    - Thm 3.3: passing KV working memory gives the same outputs as passing the predecessor's text.
    - Thm 3.4: lower per-agent complexity.
    - number: 235.7 / 377.1 / 471.4 times "more efficient" for Qwen3-4B / 8B / 14B
    - quote: "for Qwen3-4B / 8B / 14B models (Yang et al., 2025), latent thoughts generation can be 235.7 / 377.1 / 471.4 times more efficient than text-based reasoning"
    - where: p4. These are theoretical bounds, not measured speedups; the measured ones are 2.6×–7×.

11. Debuggability. A "debug mode" decodes a parallel text probe from each agent without changing what is passed on.
    - number: 96.2% (77/80) of intermediate texts are correct when the final answer is correct; 90.0% (18/20) are wrong when it is wrong.
    - setup: 100 pairs, Qwen3-14B, GSM8K, manually annotated.
    - quote: "96.2% of the intermediate text are valid when the final answer is correct, while 90.0% contain errors when the final answer contains error."
    - where: p26, Table 8

12. Diversity of latent thoughts. Mean pairwise cosine similarity of embeddings: TextMAS 0.126 / 0.142 / 0.155 against LatentMAS 0.104 / 0.093 / 0.108, at 4B / 8B / 14B (lower means more diverse).
    - setup: embedding visualisation (Figure 5) uses 300 MedQA questions, 40 latent steps, and a 4096-token budget for TextMAS.
    - where: p7–8 and p25

LIMITS
- Same-architecture assumption. Sec G: "we assume that all agents in LatentMAS share the same shape of transformer layers." Heterogeneous agents would need a "trainable adapter" (future work, not tested). The experiments use one model family per run, all agents identical.
- Needs white-box access to hidden states and the KV cache. This rules out API-only models. I infer this; the paper states it implicitly and does not list it as a limitation.
- The paper has no dedicated limitations section. It names no failure cases beyond the single debug-mode error case and the latent-step decline.
- Models are small and open (3B–14B). No frontier-scale model was tested, and there are no tool-use or long-horizon agent tasks. Only two fixed MAS topologies were tested, both with 3–4 agents.
- Accuracy gains over TextMAS are small, and some are losses (see claim 3). The TextMAS baseline is a prompted chain-of-agents. The paper does not compare against other latent or cache-sharing methods (e.g. Cache-to-Cache, KVComm) in its tables.
- It only cites Cemri et al. 2025 (why multi-agent systems fail) for the point that MAS designs vary. It does not test whether latent passing helps with coordination failures.
- Max-length caps differ by task; the "20K tokens" baseline cost depends on the 20,000 cap.
- Latent passing is not human-readable. Auditing relies on the debug-mode probe, which was validated on only 100 GSM8K cases.

BUILDS ON
- Coconut: Hao et al., 2024 (training LLMs to reason in continuous latent space), for latent generation.
- Liu et al., 2024 (differentiable cache augmentation) and Fu et al., 2025 (Cache-to-Cache), plus Zheng et al., 2025, for KV and cache exchange across models.
- Zhang et al., 2024b (chain-of-agents) for the sequential MAS, and Zhuge et al., 2024 for the hierarchical one.
- Hoerl & Kennard, 1970 (ridge regression / pseudo-inverse) for the alignment operator.
- Park et al., 2023b (linear representation hypothesis) for the expressiveness proof.
- Kwon et al., 2023 (vLLM) and HuggingFace Transformers for the serving backends.
- Benchmarks and models: Cobbe 2021 (GSM8K), Rein 2023 (GPQA), Clark 2018 (ARC), Liu 2023 (EvalPlus), Yang 2025 (Qwen3), Grattafiori 2024 (Llama 3).
- Related: Coda-Forno 2025 and Ye 2025a (latent communication that needs training).

CODE: none in the paper; the repo is linked. The Sec 3.1 equation, e = h·Wa with Wa ≈ W_out† W_in (Eq. 3, p3), is the only core formula. The prompt templates are in Appendix K, which I did not read.

FIGURES
- Fig 2 (p3): sequential and hierarchical MAS topologies. This is the quickest way to see which agent roles were tested.
- Fig 3 (p4): the LatentMAS pipeline. It shows latent thoughts, alignment, and layer-wise KV concatenation between A1, A2 and A3.
- Fig 1 (p1), Fig 4 (p6) and Fig 10 (p23): per-benchmark speed-up and token reduction bars.
- Fig 6 (p8) and Fig 11 (p25): unaligned vs aligned embedding density, which shows why Wa is needed.
- Fig 8 (p9): accuracy against latent-step count, peaking at 40–80.
I did not run the figures script, so I have not checked these captions against the extraction.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions found in the text read.
- Table cells in the extraction are run together (e.g. "99.1 98.8↓0.3", "2420581" means TextMAS 2420 tokens and LatentMAS 581). I split these by hand using the stated reduction percentages. Quotes are verbatim, but read the columns with care.
- The extraction of Theorem 3.1 shows "Ω dhm/log|V|" with garbled brackets.
- The Fig 7 per-task labels (+3.6%, +2.3%, +5.3%) were read without task names.
- Appendices I, J and K (case studies and prompts) were not read.
- The head matter has odd dates (v4 on 3 Aug 2026, "PMLR 306, 2026"), which are as printed.
